abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: We report on the randomized portion of the phase 2, open-label CheckMate 650 trial (NCT02985957), in which docetaxel-experienced, biologically male patients with chemotherapy-refractory metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer were randomized 2:2:1:2 to nivolumab 3 mg /kg plus ipilimumab 1 mg /kg (n = 73), nivolumab 1 mg /kg plus ipilimumab 3 mg /kg (n = 74), ipilimumab 3 mg /kg (n = 38), or cabazitaxel (n = 74). Primary endpoints were objective response rate and radiographic progression-free survival; key secondary endpoints included overall survival, prostate-specific antigen response rate, and safety. This portion of CheckMate 650 was not designed to statistically compare between cohorts. Respectively, objective response rates (95% CI) were 9.3% (2.6-22.1), 19.5% (8.8-34.9), 4.5% (0.1-22.8), and 12.2% (4.1-26.2), and median radiographic progression-free survival (95% CI) was 3.9 (2.2-7.6), 4.2 (3.3-5.6), 3.5 (2.1-5.8), and 7.9 (5.6-9.3) months. Respective incidence of grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events was 28.8%, 30.1%, 18.4%, and 34.7%. Preliminary post hoc biomarker analyses in patients who received treatment with any immunotherapy regimen (i.e., treated with either of the nivolumab plus ipilimumab regimens or with ipilimumab alone, n = 12) identified a transcriptional signature, derived from the most highly expressed genes across cell types within select perivascular immune niches (comprising CD31+ endothelial, CD14+HLA-DR+ myeloid, and CD4+ and CD8+ T cells), which was associated with prolonged overall survival. These results provide further evidence of antitumor activity with nivolumab plus ipilimumab in select patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer and nominate a candidate prognostic biomarker that warrants confirmation in future prospective clinical trials.

abstract.p: CheckMate 650 was a multicohort phase 2 trial designed to study the safety and clinical activity of nivolumab plus ipilimumab combination therapy in patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer. Here the authors report the results of the randomized portion of the trial, including three different immunotherapy treatment cohorts and a current standard-of-care chemotherapy cohort (cabazitaxel).

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: CheckMate 650 (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02985957) was an international, open-label, multicohort phase 2 trial designed to investigate the clinical activity and safety of nivolumab plus ipilimumab combination therapy in patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC). In preliminary analyses conducted during the signal-seeking portion of the trial, nivolumab plus ipilimumab showed antitumor activity in patients with chemotherapy-naïve and chemotherapy-refractory mCRPC, with provisional evidence of potential biomarkers of response including high tumor mutational burden (TMB)1. Nevertheless, interpretation of these results was challenging due to a high proportion of early discontinuations; ~71% of patients did not receive all four planned nivolumab plus ipilimumab combination doses, with ~38% of patients in the chemotherapy-naïve and chemotherapy-refractory cohorts discontinuing during combination dosing due to study drug toxicity1.

Patients in the signal-seeking portion of CheckMate 650 received nivolumab 1 mg /kg plus ipilimumab 3 mg /kg every 3 weeks (Q3W) for up to four doses, followed by 480 mg nivolumab every 4 weeks (Q4W)1. However, clinical studies in other tumor types have indicated the potential for efficacy and safety benefits using an alternative nivolumab plus ipilimumab regimen (dosing at 3 mg/kg and 1 mg/kg, respectively) and/or by administering the ipilimumab component less frequently (dosing every 6 weeks [Q6W] vs Q3W)2,3. As a result, the randomized portion of CheckMate 650 was designed to include three different immunotherapy treatment cohorts and a standard-of-care cohort for patients with postchemotherapy mCRPC. There were two cohorts investigating alternative nivolumab plus ipilimumab dosing regimens, one cohort investigating ipilimumab monotherapy, and one investigating standard-of-care cabazitaxel.

Here, we present results from the randomized portion of CheckMate 650 that show further evidence of antitumor activity with nivolumab plus ipilimumab in select patients with postchemotherapy mCRPC and provisionally identify a transcriptional signature that may be associated with prolonged overall survival (OS) in patients with mCRPC.

sec.title: Patients and treatment
sec.p: Between 20 August 2019 and 5 October 2021, 259 eligible biologically male patients were randomized to either nivolumab 3 mg/kg plus ipilimumab 1 mg/kg Q3W for up to four doses, followed by 480 mg nivolumab Q4W, with the first nivolumab maintenance dose administered 3 weeks after the last combination dose (the N3I1 cohort, n = 73); nivolumab 1 mg/kg Q3W for up to eight doses plus ipilimumab 3 mg/kg Q6W for up to four doses, followed by 480 mg nivolumab Q4W, with the first nivolumab maintenance dose administered 6 weeks after the last combination dose (the N1I3 cohort, n = 74); ipilimumab 3 mg/kg Q3W for up to four doses (the I-mono cohort, n = 38); or cabazitaxel 20 or 25 mg/m2 Q3W in combination with oral prednisone or prednisolone 10 mg/day for up to 10 doses (the CABA cohort, n = 74) (Fig. 1). Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics for all randomized patients are shown in Supplementary Table 1. Across the cohorts, most patients were aged ≥65 years, White, with a Gleason score >7 and ≥4 bone lesions. The overall study population was relatively heavily pretreated, with the most common previous systemic therapies administered in any metastatic setting being docetaxel with or without prednisone/prednisolone, enzalutamide, and abiraterone plus prednisone/prednisolone. There were noteworthy differences between the cohorts in some baseline characteristics, including higher hemoglobin levels in the N3I1 cohort, lower average daily worst pain intensity and higher median prostate-specific antigen (PSA) in the N1I3 cohort, and lower age and a higher proportion of Black or African American patients in the I-mono cohort. The cohorts also tended to vary in terms of baseline lactate dehydrogenase and alkaline phosphatase levels (Supplementary Table 1). Treatment was administered to all 73 patients randomized to the N3I1 cohort, 73 of the 74 patients randomized to the N1I3 cohort, all 38 patients randomized to the I-mono cohort, and 72 of the 74 patients randomized to the CABA cohort. At the time of data cutoff for this analysis (16 June 2022), 4 of the 73 treated patients (5.5%) in each nivolumab plus ipilimumab cohort were continuing treatment; no patients were continuing treatment with ipilimumab monotherapy or cabazitaxel (Supplementary Table 2). Primary reasons for treatment discontinuation in the N3I1 and N1I3 cohorts were disease progression (n = 39, 53.4% and n = 29, 39.7%, respectively) or study drug toxicity (n = 11, 15.1% and n = 19, 26.0%). In the I-mono cohort, 19 patients (50.0%) completed ipilimumab treatment, while 11 (28.9%) and 3 (7.9%) discontinued due to disease progression and study drug toxicity, respectively. Among treated patients in the CABA cohort, 25 (34.7%) completed cabazitaxel treatment, and 28 (38.9%) and 5 (6.9%) discontinued due to disease progression and study drug toxicity (Supplementary Table 2). In total, 12 of the 38 patients (31.6%) randomized to the I-mono cohort and 25 of the 74 patients (33.8%) randomized to the CABA cohort crossed over to the N3I1 cohort following disease progression. Subsequent anticancer therapies for all cohorts are summarized in Supplementary Table 3.

sec.p: Discontinuations due to study drug toxicity during nivolumab plus ipilimumab combination dosing are summarized in Supplementary Table 4. Overall, 11 of 73 treated patients (15.1%) in the N3I1 cohort and 22 of 73 treated patients (30.1%) in the N1I3 cohort did not receive all four combination doses due to study drug toxicity. Nine patients (12.3%) in the N3I1 cohort and 17 (23.3%) in the N1I3 cohort discontinued and did not receive further study treatment; an additional 2 patients in the N3I1 cohort (2.7%) and 5 in the N1I3 cohort (6.8%) discontinued but subsequently received nivolumab maintenance monotherapy.

Treatment exposure is summarized in Supplementary Table 5. Median (range) duration of therapy among treated patients in the N3I1, N1I3, I-mono, and CABA cohorts was 2.8 (0.0–25.8), 2.4 (0.0–18.8), 2.1 (0.0–3.6), and 4.4 (0.7–7.9) months, respectively. During combination dosing, the median (range) number of doses received in the N3I1 and N1I3 cohorts was 4.0 (1.0–4.0) and 4.0 (1.0–8.0) for nivolumab, and 4.0 (1.0–4.0) and 2.0 (1.0–4.0) for ipilimumab. In the I-mono cohort, the median (range) number of ipilimumab doses received was 3.5 (1.0–4.0). In the CABA cohort, the median (range) number of cabazitaxel doses received was 6.0 (1.0–10.0). Overall, 37 of 73 treated patients (50.7%) in the N3I1 cohort and 12 of 73 treated patients (16.4%) in the N1I3 cohort subsequently received nivolumab maintenance monotherapy, with the respective median (range) number of doses being 5.0 (1.0–24.0) and 6.5 (2.0–14.0) (Supplementary Table 5).

sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p: Among patients with baseline measurable disease per the case report form (CRF), objective response rate (ORR) per blinded independent central review (BICR) was 9.3% in the N3I1 cohort, 19.5% in the N1I3 cohort, 4.5% in the I-mono cohort, and 12.2% in the CABA cohort (Table 1). Complete responses were reported in one patient (2.3%) in the N3I1 cohort and two patients (4.9%) in the N1I3 cohort; no patients in the I-mono or CABA cohorts achieved a complete response. Median time to objective response was approximately 2.0 months in both the N3I1 and N1I3 cohorts, with median duration of response not reached in either cohort. In the I-mono and CABA cohorts, median time to objective response was 2.0 and 3.8 months, respectively, with a median duration of response of 6.5 months in both cohorts (Table 1). Overall disease control rates (proportions with complete response, partial response, or stable disease) were 46.5%, 51.2%, 45.5%, and 73.2% for the N3I1, N1I3, I-mono, and CABA cohorts, respectively. Exposure data by objective response per BICR are provided for the N3I1 and N1I3 cohorts in Supplementary Table 6. Additional detailed information for the 12 patients in the N3I1 and N1I3 cohorts with objective responses per BICR are provided in Table 2. Objective response outcomes for patients with baseline measurable disease per the interactive web response system (IWRS) are shown for all cohorts in Supplementary Table 7 and were comparable with those described above for patients with baseline measurable disease per the CRF.

sec.p: Among the PSA-evaluable population, the confirmed PSA response rate (PSA-RR) was 13.8% in the N3I1 cohort, 18.2% in the N1I3 cohort, 5.4% in the I-mono cohort, and 23.9% in the CABA cohort (Table 1). Median time to confirmed PSA response was 0.8 months in both the N3I1 and N1I3 cohorts, with median duration of confirmed PSA response not reached in either cohort. Median time to confirmed PSA response was 1.5 months in both the I-mono and CABA cohorts, with respective median durations of confirmed PSA response of 14.2 and 5.8 months (Table 1). Median time to PSA progression (95% CI) in all randomized patients was 3.3 (2.9–4.2), 4.4 (3.2–5.6), 3.8 (3.2–4.7), and 4.2 (3.1–6.1) months in the N3I1, N1I3, I-mono, and CABA cohorts, respectively. Waterfall plots of maximum percentage change from baseline in tumor size and PSA are shown in Fig. 2. A > 75% maximum reduction in tumor size was observed in 3 of 33 (9.1%), 4 of 31 (12.9%), 0 of 20 (0.0%), and 0 of 35 (0.0%) evaluable patients in the N3I1, N1I3, I-mono, and CABA cohorts, respectively (Fig. 2a). A > 80% maximum reduction in PSA was observed in 8 of 65 (12.3%), 9 of 66 (13.6%), 3 of 37 (8.1%), and 7 of 71 (9.9%) evaluable patients, respectively (Fig. 2b).

sec.p: Median radiographic progression-free survival (rPFS) (95% CI) per BICR in all randomized patients was 3.9 (2.2–7.6), 4.2 (3.3–5.6), 3.5 (2.1–5.8), and 7.9 (5.6–9.3) months in the N3I1, N1I3, I-mono, and CABA cohorts, respectively (Fig. 3a). After a median (range) follow-up of 23.3 (6.0–31.5) months for OS, median OS (95% CI) in all randomized patients was 15.9 (12.8–17.7), 13.5 (10.4–16.7), 18.5 (10.7-not estimable), and 14.8 (11.4–16.0) months, respectively, with 12-month OS rates of 64.9%, 53.1%, 66.8% and 59.9% (Fig. 3b).

sec.p: Across the cohorts, baseline tissue TMB data were available from 134 of 256 patient samples (52.3%) and blood TMB data from 183 of 257 patient samples (71.2%). Supplementary Tables 8 and 9 detail efficacy outcomes in patients with high and low baseline tissue or blood TMB based either on study population medians or receiver operating characteristic curve analyses. In the N3I1 cohort, ORRs and PSA-RRs were consistently higher among patients with high baseline tissue or blood TMB, regardless of the cutoff used. Similar results were observed for rPFS and OS for tissue TMB, although differences between high and low TMB subgroups for blood TMB were less consistent and, in some cases, numerically marginal (Supplementary Tables 8 and 9, Supplementary Fig. 1). For the N1I3, I-mono, and CABA cohorts, there was no consistent relationship between tissue or blood TMB and clinical activity, with improved efficacy outcomes sometimes observed in the high TMB subgroups and sometimes in the low TMB subgroups, depending on the endpoint, TMB type (tissue vs blood) and applied cutoff (Supplementary Tables 8 and 9, Supplementary Fig. 1).

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: Treatment-related adverse events (AEs) of any grade occurred in 55 (75.3%; grade ≥3: 21, 28.8%), 58 (79.5%; grade ≥3: 22, 30.1%), 27 (71.1%; grade ≥3: 7, 18.4%), and 58 (80.6%; grade ≥3: 25, 34.7%) treated patients in the N3I1, N1I3, I-mono and CABA cohorts, respectively (Table 3). The most common grade ≥3 treatment-related AEs were diarrhea (n = 6, 8.2%), fatigue, and increased lipase (n = 3 for each, 4.1%) in the N3I1 cohort, and diarrhea (n = 6, 8.2%), immune-mediated enterocolitis (n = 5, 6.8%), colitis, and hypophysitis (n = 3 for each, 4.1%) in the N1I3 cohort. In the I-mono cohort, only one treatment-related AE occurred at grade ≥3 in more than one patient (immune-mediated enterocolitis in two patients, 5.3%). In the CABA cohort, the most common grade ≥3 treatment-related AEs were anemia (n = 6, 8.3%), decreased neutrophil count (n = 4, 5.6%), fatigue, neutropenia, and febrile neutropenia (n = 3 for each, 4.2%; Table 3).

sec.p: Treatment-related AEs of any grade led to discontinuation in 11 (15.1%; grade ≥3: 9, 12.3%), 19 (26.0%; grade ≥3: 16, 21.9%), 3 (7.9%; grade ≥3: 2, 5.3%), and 6 (8.3%; grade ≥3: 3, 4.2%) treated patients in the N3I1, N1I3, I-mono, and CABA cohorts, respectively. Patients discontinuing treatment in the N3I1, N1I3, or I-mono cohorts due to grade ≥3 treatment-related AEs did so mostly because of gastrointestinal disorders, such as diarrhea and colitis (5 of 9 patients in the N3I1 cohort, 9 of 16 in the N1I3 cohort, and both patients in the I-mono cohort).

Immune-mediated AEs reported across the N3I1, N1I3, and I-mono cohorts were predominantly endocrine, gastrointestinal, or skin-related (Supplementary Table 10). The most common individual grade ≥3 immune-mediated AEs were diarrhea (n = 4, 5.5%) in the N3I1 cohort, immune-mediated enterocolitis (n = 7, 9.6%) in the N1I3 cohort, and both hypophysitis and immune-mediated enterocolitis (n = 2 for each, 5.3%) in the I-mono cohort. High-dose corticosteroids ( ≥ 40 mg prednisone or equivalent) were required for immune-mediated AEs in 15 (20.5%), 25 (34.2%), and 6 (15.8%) patients in the N3I1, N1I3, and I-mono cohorts, respectively.

Two deaths were considered related to study drug toxicity. One patient in the N3I1 cohort died within 30 days of last dose of study drug due to immune-mediated pneumonitis; one patient in the N1I3 cohort died more than 100 days after last dose of study drug due to immune-mediated colitis.

sec.title: CODEX assay and analyses
sec.p: To evaluate candidate molecular biomarkers of response, patients were segregated into exceptional responders and nonresponders. Exceptional responders were those who met ≥3 of the following five criteria: (1) objective radiographic response by Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) v1.1 with Prostate Cancer Working Group 3 (PCWG3) modifications (complete or partial response); (2) percentage decrease in sum of diameters of radiographic target lesions of ≥30%; (3) confirmed ≥50% decline in serum PSA; (4) rPFS >12 months; (5) OS > 18 months. Among the patients with available tumor tissue, tissue sections were obtained from pretreatment tumor biopsies of primary prostate tumors (total n = 8 [responders n = 4, nonresponders n = 4]) or soft-tissue metastatic sites (total n = 4 [responders n = 3, nonresponders n = 1]) in 12 patients who received treatment with any immunotherapy regimen (N3I1, N1I3, and I-mono). The median time from sample collection to start of immunotherapy (interquartile range [IQR]) for the primary prostate tumors (total n = 8) was 3.0 (0.7–29.3) months. The median time from sample collection to start of immunotherapy (IQR) for the soft-tissue metastatic samples (total n = 4) was 4.5 (0.8–10.8) months.

To define the composition and spatial organization of cellular subtypes within the tumor microenvironment (TME) in responders versus nonresponders, spatial proteomics was performed using co-detection by indexing (CODEX) with a panel of 53 protein markers encompassing immune, epithelial, stromal, vascular, and other cell types (Supplementary Tables 11 and 12). After cell segmentation and quality control filtering, distinct clusters were identified and validated through unsupervised clustering, followed by manual cell-type annotations. Distinct cellular niches comprising CD31+ blood vessels surrounded by CD14+ myeloid cells, CD8+ and CD4+ T cells, and CD11c+ dendritic cells were identified in primary (Fig. 4a) and metastatic prostate cancers (Supplementary Fig. 2). The density of these perivascular immune niches was significantly higher in pretreatment primary prostate tumors in responders compared with nonresponders (P = 0.028) (Fig. 4a).

Assessment of perivascular immune niche density showed significantly higher niches (P = 0.0286, Mann–Whitney paired t test) to be present in responder (n = 4) when compared with nonresponder cases (n = 4). Box plots represent the median, range and the whiskers represent minima and maxima range. b Cell-to-cell interactions were performed on responder cases (n = 4) and nonresponders cases (n = 4). Cell interactions between all cellular subsets showed significant interaction of the CD14+ HLA-DR+ myeloid cells with (1) CD4+ T cells (P = 0.015), (2) CD8 + CD44 + T cells (P = 0.018), and (3) CD31+ endothelial cell (P = 0.027, Welch’s unpaired t test). Data are presented as mean values +/− SEM. c Kaplan–Meier plot showing overall survival of prostate cancer patients from the TCGA database with above (red, high expression; n = 242 patients) or below (blue, low expression; n = 242 patients) median expression of the seven gene signatures. P values and hazard ratio (HR) are displayed. Source data are provided as a Source Data file. CODEX, co-detection by indexing; NR, nonresponders; R, responders; SEM, standard error of the mean; TCGA, The Cancer Gene Atlas; TME, tumor microenvironment.

sec.p: Among these cellular subsets within spatial proximity of each other in the primary prostate TME, we confirmed significantly higher interaction proportions between CD14+ HLA-DR+ antigen presenting myeloid cells with (1) CD4+ T cells (P = 0.015), (2) CD8+ CD44+ T cells (P = 0.018), and (3) CD31+ endothelial cells (P = 0.027) in responders versus nonresponders (Fig. 4b). No significant interaction was observed with CD11c+ dendritic cells (data not shown). These aggregates of CD8+ and CD4+ T cells with CD14+ myeloid cells around endothelial cells comprise perivascular immune niches that may be predictive of response.

To externally test these perivascular immune niches associated with clinical response, we derived a transcriptional signature from the top five differentially expressed genes across cell types identified by the CODEX assay using the single-cell prostate cancer reference4, including more specifically defined cell types such as monocytes, endothelial cells, dendritic cells, CD4 naïve/central memory T cells, cytotoxic CD8 T cells, CD4 memory T cells, and CD8 memory T cells. This simplified signature was intended to capture the most abundant cell types identified by the spatial analyses. We tested this signature within primary prostate tumor cohorts in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA). Gene set variation analysis was applied to evaluate the expression levels of these genes in the TCGA-PRAD dataset with patients dichotomized based on the median value. We found that patients with high expression of this gene signature had prolonged OS compared with patients with low expression (hazard ratio 1.21, P = 0.037) (Fig. 4c). Taken together, the findings indicated that these perivascular immune niches may represent a prognostic biomarker, and further investigation may help determine if these are also predictive for response to immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy in patients with mCRPC.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Preliminary data from the signal-seeking portion of CheckMate 650 suggested that nivolumab 1 mg/kg plus ipilimumab 3 mg/kg administered Q3W for up to four doses has antitumor activity in chemotherapy-naïve and chemotherapy-refractory mCRPC; however, these outcomes were confounded by study drug toxicity and a related high incidence of early discontinuations1. The results reported here from the randomized portion of CheckMate 650 assessing alternative dosing schedules of nivolumab plus ipilimumab provide further information on the safety and efficacy of this combination regimen in patients with chemotherapy-refractory mCRPC.

Safety profiles for treatments administered across the four cohorts were as expected based on previous clinical studies in mCRPC or other tumor types1,2,5–10, with the most common grade ≥3 treatment-related AEs generally being gastrointestinal events with nivolumab plus ipilimumab and ipilimumab monotherapy, and hematological with cabazitaxel. While the study was not designed to compare safety, the incidence of treatment-related AEs appeared relatively consistent across the cohorts. However, the frequency of grade ≥3 treatment-related AEs was numerically higher in the N3I1, N1I3, and CABA cohorts versus the I-mono cohort and the proportion of patients discontinuing due to treatment-related AEs was numerically higher in the N3I1 and N1I3 cohorts than in the I-mono and CABA cohorts. Between the two nivolumab plus ipilimumab regimens, the proportion of patients who discontinued before receipt of all of four combination doses due to study drug toxicity was higher in the N1I3 cohort versus the N3I1 cohort, as was the proportion discontinuing at any time due to grade ≥3 treatment-related AEs. This perhaps suggests that the N3I1 regimen was more tolerable than the N1I3 regimen. However, the respective rates of discontinuation may have been influenced by ipilimumab being dosed Q3W for the N3I1 regimen and Q6W for the N1I3 regimen, meaning the respective timeframe of combination dosing was shorter in the N3I1 cohort (12 weeks) versus the N1I3 cohort (24 weeks). Nevertheless, as anticipated, both dosing schedules adopted for the randomized portion of CheckMate 650 appeared to provide safety/tolerability improvements versus the regimen used in the signal-seeking portion (nivolumab 1 mg/kg plus ipilimumab 3 mg/kg Q3W for up to four doses), which resulted in ~38% of chemotherapy-experienced patients discontinuing before receipt of all four combination doses and ~27% discontinuing at any time due to grade ≥3 treatment-related AEs1.

An encouraging observation from the two nivolumab plus ipilimumab cohorts was that some patients achieved objective and PSA responses that appeared to be both deep (complete objective responses were seen in the N3I1 and N1I3 cohorts, and most objective responders achieved notable reductions in tumor size and PSA) and durable (durations of objective and PSA responses were not reached in the N3I1 and N1I3 cohorts). We note that although the study was not statistically powered to compare between cohorts, the observed ORR was below the expected ORR of approximately 30% in the N3I1 and/or N1I3 cohorts (based on a two-sided 95% CI of 16.8% to 45.2%, with the lower bound above the approximately 15% expected response rate for cabazitaxel based on the TROPIC study8).

We conducted additional evaluations of the 12 patients who achieved an objective response with nivolumab plus ipilimumab to determine whether there were any consistent pre- or on-treatment characteristics across these objective responders but found no clear patterns. Patients with objective response showed variations in the types and number of previous systemic therapies received in the metastatic setting, the size of target soft-tissue lesions, baseline PSA levels and tissue and blood TMB values, and the types and number of high-grade treatment-related AEs. Of interest, when nivolumab plus ipilimumab exposure data were assessed by objective response outcomes, no substantial differences were found between the groups of patients achieving a response, not achieving a response, or without baseline measurable disease, suggesting that the number of combination doses received is, likewise, not associated with response. Although no common characteristics were observed across the objective responders, it was noted that tumor responses appeared to be associated with both PSA responses and improved survival outcomes. For example, all four patients in the N3I1 cohort who had an objective response also had notable PSA reductions (three had 100% PSA reduction and one had >80% reduction), and three of the four patients had no recorded progression event and were alive and on treatment at database lock. In the N1I3 cohort, five of the eight patients with an objective response also had notable PSA reductions (all had 100% PSA reduction), and five of the eight patients had no recorded progression event and were alive at database lock (two were still on treatment and three were in follow-up). More in-depth correlative and biomarker analyses are required to further investigate any common characteristics of patients with chemotherapy-refractory mCRPC who respond to nivolumab plus ipilimumab combination therapy.

As expected from prior clinical trials in mCRPC populations, ipilimumab monotherapy and cabazitaxel showed antitumor activity in this study. The results observed in the I-mono cohort varied in part from those reported in a large-scale, phase 3 trial of ipilimumab monotherapy after radiotherapy for postchemotherapy mCRPC. In that trial, the PSA-RR was 13%, median PFS was 4.0 months, and median OS was 11.2 months5. While the median PFS in the I-mono cohort (3.5 months) was comparable to that previously reported, the PSA-RR was lower (5.4%), which may reflect the lower dose of ipilimumab used here (3 mg/kg) versus the prior study (10 mg/kg) and/or the addition of radiation therapy. Moreover, the longer median OS seen in the I-mono cohort (18.5 months) may be due to the crossover study design, the addition of radiation therapy, and/or subsequent systemic therapies received in that cohort. Results for the CABA cohort were not markedly dissimilar from those previously reported in three large scale trials of cabazitaxel 25 mg/m2 for patients with post-docetaxel mCRPC8–10. In those studies, ORRs ranged from 14%–37%, PSA-RRs from 36%–43%, PFS medians from 2.8–4.4 months, and OS medians from 13.6–15.1 months8,10. Although the PFS and OS medians reported for the CABA cohort (7.9 and 14.8 months, respectively) were relatively aligned with these prior results, the ORR and PSA-RR were slightly lower (12.2% and 23.9%, respectively). This may reflect differing study designs and patient populations, as well as the potential influence of some patients in the CABA cohort receiving the 20 mg/m2 dose, which has previously been associated with lower response rates versus the 25 mg/m2 dose9.

Although the randomized portion of CheckMate 650 provides insights into the efficacy of the four treatment regimens, comparisons across the cohorts should not be performed. There are several reasons for this, including (1) this portion of the trial was not designed to statistically compare efficacy outcomes across the treatments; (2) there were several imbalances between the cohorts, such as the lower proportion of patients with baseline anemia in the N3I1 cohort, the lower proportion with high average daily worst pain intensity and the higher median PSA in the N1I3 cohort, the higher proportion of Black or African American patients in the I-mono cohort, and the general variability in baseline prognostic laboratory tests such as lactate dehydrogenase and alkaline phosphatase levels, which could have differentially influenced efficacy outcomes in this study11–19; and (3) OS outcomes in the I-mono and CABA cohorts may have been confounded by approximately one-third of the patients (31.6% of patients in the I-mono cohort and 33.8% of patients in the CABA cohort) crossing over to the N3I1 cohort, as well as any subsequent anticancer therapies received by the 35%–50% of patients who discontinued due to completing their course of ipilimumab monotherapy (maximum of four doses) or cabazitaxel treatment (maximum of 10 doses). Comparison of the efficacy of these treatments would require an additional prospectively designed and adequately powered study.

Based on preliminary results from the signal-seeking portion of CheckMate 650 showing improved clinical activity in small patient groups with high tissue TMB1, we assessed associations between TMB derived from both tumor tissue and blood samples and efficacy outcomes across the four cohorts. In a limited number of evaluable patients, a potential relationship between improved antitumor activity and high tissue TMB, and to a lesser extent high blood TMB, was observed for the N3I1 cohort. However, there was no consistent relationship between tissue or blood TMB and any of the assessed efficacy endpoints in the N1I3, I-mono, or CABA cohorts, regardless of the TMB cutoffs employed. This is inconsistent with the results obtained from the signal-seeking portion of the study, which utilized a similar N1I3 dosing regimen1. Published data on associations between TMB and clinical activity of immunotherapy-based treatment in mCRPC have been mixed20–24. Assessing a potential role for TMB in response to immunotherapy-based treatment in patients with mCRPC is challenging as prostate cancer has a relatively low overall mutational burden versus other tumor types25. Furthermore, there is no established threshold for high TMB in mCRPC, and cutoffs vary across reported studies1,21–23. It is also noteworthy that the data on associations between TMB and efficacy of immunotherapy-based treatment in mCRPC are from relatively small sample sizes. In the present analyses, TMB data were only available from between ~50% (for tissue TMB) and ~70% (for blood TMB) of patients, resulting in small and highly variable individual category sizes across the evaluable subpopulations (range, n = 4 to n = 46). In addition, concordance between tissue and blood next-generation sequencing assays has been reported to vary by tumor type, as well as the specific genes assessed26. Ultimately, larger prospectively designed studies are necessary to appropriately determine whether tissue and/or blood TMB influences response to nivolumab plus ipilimumab in patients with mCRPC.

As TMB is intrinsic to tumor epithelial cells only, we sought to define a more comprehensive TME biomarker incorporating immune and stromal components. Spatial proteomics analyses of the pretreatment prostate TME revealed CD14+ myeloid, CD8+ and CD4+ T cells, and CD11c+ dendritic cells aggregated around blood vessels forming perivascular immune niches. These niches could potentially play a role in priming antitumor immune responses. These interactions have been previously reported to support an antitumoral response27. By externally validating these findings in a separate cohort of patients with prostate cancer who were predominantly untreated with immunotherapy, these perivascular immune cell niches in the pretreatment TME and the derivative transcriptional signature may potentially serve as both a prognostic and/or predictive biomarker for response to immune checkpoint inhibitor therapies. We acknowledge the small sample size for the biomarker analysis; these results are intended to be hypothesis-generating for subsequent validation in larger, prospective trials, including evaluation in patients treated with and without immunotherapy. A potential limitation of the biomarker analysis is the fact that mCRPC emerges after several years of hormonal therapy and under the pharmacologic pressure of multiple drugs (e.g., in many cases, androgen receptor pathway inhibitors and taxane-based chemotherapies). One approach to overcome this limitation is the development of liquid biopsies (i.e., evaluation of cell-free DNA, extracellular vesicles, or circulating cells) that permit longitudinal and noninvasive assessment at multiple timepoints.

In summary, CheckMate 650 represents one of the largest prospective trials evaluating the potential efficacy and safety of immunotherapy in mCRPC, with data from the randomized portion providing additional information on the antitumor activity of nivolumab plus ipilimumab in select patients with chemotherapy-refractory mCRPC. Importantly, it also represents the largest prospective randomized trial of post-docetaxel immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy and cabazitaxel in patients with mCRPC, thus representing an important step in improving our understanding of the safety/efficacy of these agents relative to chemotherapy. The results also suggest that the newly tested nivolumab plus ipilimumab dosing regimens may be more tolerable than the regimen previously evaluated in the signal-seeking portion of the study. Overall, these data contribute to our further understanding of a potential role for immunotherapy-based regimens in the treatment of select patients with mCRPC21–23,28–31. Additionally, preliminary biomarker analyses nominated perivascular immune niches and a derivative gene signature in pretreatment tumor tissues as a candidate prognostic and/or predictive biomarker of response. Future clinical trials should incorporate these pretreatment tissue biomarkers alongside investigation of non-invasive liquid biopsy strategies to optimize patient selection. Advanced ctDNA analyses, including fragmentomics; methylation-based assays, such as enzymatic methyl-seq (EM-seq); and circulating histone modification profiling, can capture tumor-specific epigenetic and chromatin features, offering dynamic and complementary insights beyond tissue-based biomarkers.

sec.title: Study design and participants
sec.p: The open-label, multicohort phase 2 CheckMate 650 trial was first registered with ClinicalTrials.gov on 22 November 2016 (NCT02985957), and was conducted in accordance with consensus ethical principles derived from international guidelines including the Declaration of Helsinki, Council for International Organizations of Medical Sciences, and Good Clinical Practice, as defined by the International Conference on Harmonisation. All patients provided written informed consent. The trial protocol was approved by the institutional review board and/or ethics committee for participating sites in Australia, Austria, Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, Poland, Spain, and the USA (Supplementary Table 13). All protocol amendments are detailed in the latest version of the protocol, provided in the Supplementary Information, and available online at https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/57/NCT02985957/Prot_SAP_000.pdf. Enrollment into the randomized portion of the CheckMate 650 trial was conducted between 5 August 2019 and 8 September 2021.

The study design for the signal-seeking portion of CheckMate 650 has been described previously1. After protocol revisions in February 2019 and March 2020, four new cohorts were established to evaluate two alternative nivolumab plus ipilimumab dosing regimens, ipilimumab monotherapy, and cabazitaxel plus prednisone/prednisolone in patients with postchemotherapy mCRPC, as part of the randomized portion of the trial. As described previously1, key overall study inclusion criteria were age ≥18 years, histological confirmation of adenocarcinoma of the prostate with evidence of metastatic disease, ongoing androgen deprivation therapy with a gonadotropin-releasing hormone analog or bilateral orchiectomy confirmed by testosterone ≤1.73 nmol/L (50 ng/dL) at screening, tumor progression while receiving androgen deprivation therapy per Prostate Cancer Working Group 2 (PCWG2) criteria, and an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0-1. Inclusion was also contingent on availability of sufficient tumor samples for biomarker analyses (fresh biopsy or archival tissue collected within 1 year before enrollment). Key overall study exclusion criteria were visceral liver metastases; active brain or leptomeningeal metastases; active, known, or suspected autoimmune disease; corticosteroid/immunosuppressant use within 14 days of start of study treatment; and prior treatment targeting T-cell co-stimulation or immune checkpoint pathways. For enrollment into the new cohorts, patients were also required to have progressed after prior docetaxel-containing therapy with no more than two prior chemotherapy regimens in the metastatic setting. If the docetaxel-containing therapy was received in the metastatic castration-sensitive setting, patients must also have progressed on prior second-generation hormone therapy. Additional exclusion criteria specific to the new cohorts were prior treatment with cabazitaxel in the metastatic setting, grade >2 symptomatic peripheral neuropathy, and a history of severe (grade >2) hypersensitivity to docetaxel or polysorbate 80. Because of the nature of prostate cancer, the study was only conducted in biologically male patients.

sec.title: Treatment
sec.p: Eligible patients were randomized 2:2:1:2 to the N3I1, N1I3, I-mono, or CABA cohorts. Randomization was performed using an interactive response technologies web-based system with stratification by the presence or absence of measurable disease per investigator assessment. The randomization procedures were carried out via permuted blocks within each stratum. Nivolumab and ipilimumab were administered as 30-min intravenous infusions; cabazitaxel was administered as 1-h intravenous infusions. Selection between the 20 or 25 mg /m2 dose of cabazitaxel was at the investigator’s discretion and according to country-specific labeling; however, patients with mild hepatic impairment (total bilirubin >1 to ≤1.5× upper limit of normal or aspartate aminotransferase >1.5× upper limit of normal) had to start cabazitaxel at the 20 mg/m2 dose. Patients who received ≥1 dose of either nivolumab plus ipilimumab regimen and who experienced treatment-related AEs that did not meet discontinuation criteria could begin nivolumab maintenance before completing all four ipilimumab doses on a case-by-case basis. Patients randomized to the I-mono and CABA cohorts who experienced radiographic progression as confirmed per BICR were eligible to cross over to the N3I1 cohort.

In all cohorts, treatment continued until progression, unacceptable toxicity, withdrawal of consent, or the end of the study, with the following caveats: (1) in the N3I1 and N1I3 cohorts, treatment was stopped after a maximum of 2 years; (2) in the I-mono cohort, treatment was stopped after a maximum of four ipilimumab doses. Patients treated with either nivolumab plus ipilimumab regimen or with ipilimumab monotherapy were permitted to continue treatment beyond initial radiographic progression defined by RECIST v1.1 for soft-tissue lesions or PCWG2 for bone lesions. Patients treated with cabazitaxel were not permitted to receive treatment beyond progression. Patients who met progressive disease criteria as assessed by the investigator were allowed to continue with study therapy as long as they met the following additional criteria (after consultation with the medical monitor): (1) investigator-assessed clinical benefit; (2) tolerance of study treatment; (3) stable performance status; (4) treatment beyond progression would not delay an imminent intervention to prevent serious complications of disease progression (e.g., central nervous system metastases); and (5) written informed consent was obtained before receiving additional nivolumab plus ipilimumab or nivolumab monotherapy treatment (all other elements of the main consent including description of reasonably foreseeable risks or discomforts, or other alternative treatment options will still apply). No dose increases were allowed for any study treatment. Dose reductions were permitted only for cabazitaxel when deemed necessary by the investigator, and were based on the following criteria: (1) the dose that was reduced for toxicity could not be re-escalated; and (2) up to a maximum of two dose reductions were allowed per patient (Supplementary Table 14). If a third cabazitaxel dose reduction was required, study treatment was discontinued. Dose delays and discontinuation for AEs were permitted for all study treatments. For the N3I1 and N1I3 cohorts, if dosing was delayed, both nivolumab and ipilimumab were delayed together (and subsequently resumed together).

sec.title: Endpoints and assessments
sec.p: Coprimary endpoints were ORR (the proportion of patients with measurable disease at baseline achieving a confirmed complete or partial response using RECIST v1.1) and rPFS (time from date of randomization to first documented progression [using RECIST v1.1 for soft tissue disease and PCWG2 criteria for bone lesions] or death in all randomized patients with no censoring for subsequent systemic anticancer therapy) as assessed per BICR. Key secondary endpoints included OS, PSA-RR (the proportion of randomized patients with a baseline plus ≥1 postbaseline PSA assessment achieving a PSA decline ≥50% from baseline), and safety. Per the study protocol, the coprimary ORR endpoint was based on patients with measurable disease at baseline as entered in the IWRS. However, as there was a > 5% discrepancy in the numbers of patients with measurable disease at baseline as entered in the IWRS versus entered in the CRF, a sensitivity analysis of ORR was performed on patients with measurable disease at baseline as entered in the CRF.

Preplanned exploratory endpoints included time to and duration of objective response; time to PSA progression (time from randomization to the date of PSA progression per PCWG2 criteria in all randomized patients with censoring for subsequent systemic anticancer therapy); time to and duration of confirmed PSA response; disease control rate (the proportion of randomized patients with a minimum follow-up of 6 months achieving a confirmed complete response, confirmed partial response, or stable disease per BICR); and associations between efficacy outcomes and TMB. Baseline TMB was derived either from tumor tissue or circulating tumor DNA in blood plasma. Tissue TMB, defined as the number of missense mutations per exome, was derived from whole exome sequencing of genomic DNA extracted from pretreatment tumor tissue; whole-blood DNA from the same patient was used as the germline DNA control (performed by Q2 Solutions, Durham, NC, USA). Blood TMB, defined as the number of mutations (including single-nucleotide variants, splice-site variants, insertions, deletions, amplifications, and fusions) per megabase, was derived from the GuardantOMNI gene panel (Guardant Health, Redwood City, CA, USA) using cell-free DNA extracted from the plasma of whole blood specimens collected at cycle 1 day 1 (C1D1) or at screening (up to 28 days before C1D1) in Streck Cell-Free DNA BCT Tubes. Measurements were taken from distinct samples and no samples were measured repeatedly. For the reported analyses, high and low TMB cutoffs were based either on study population medians or receiver operating characteristic curve analyses. Efficacy outcomes based on TMB were calculated using the respective evaluable populations.

The human tissue samples used in the reported analyses were collected according to patient informed consent, per the study protocol. The protocol allowed for residual sample storage for additional research. All requests for access to samples or data for additional research will be vetted as described in the Data Availability statement in this article. Any residual blood and tissue collections have been retained by the Bristol Myers Squibb Biorepository or at a Bristol Myers Squibb-approved third-party storage management facility and will be stored for 15 years or the maximum allowed by applicable law.

AEs were graded per National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events v4.0 and are reported between first dose and 30 days after last dose of study drug. Immune-mediated AEs, defined as events consistent with an immune-mediated mechanism or component for which noninflammatory etiologies (e.g., infection or tumor progression) had been ruled out but including events with an alternate etiology that were exacerbated by the induction of autoimmunity, are reported between first dose and 100 days after last dose of study drug.

Body imaging assessments were performed by contrast-enhanced CT or MRI at baseline, every 8 weeks ( ± 7 days) from first dose for the first 6 months, then every 12 weeks ( ± 7 days) until disease progression or treatment discontinuation. Tc99m-based radionuclide bone scans were conducted on the same schedule. Brain imaging (with or without contrast) was performed by MRI (or CT if MRI is contraindicated) at baseline and approximately every 12 weeks thereafter in patients with a history of brain metastasis or symptoms. PSA was assessed locally up to 6 weeks before randomization, on day 1 of cycles 1-5, then on day 1 of every subsequent odd-numbered cycle (cycle 7, cycle 9, etc.). PSA responses were confirmed by a second consecutive assessment performed at least 3 weeks later (the date of PSA response was based on first response, not the date of confirmation). Patients were followed for safety and OS after treatment discontinuation.

sec.title: Statistical analyses
sec.p: The CheckMate 650 trial is based on an overarching hypothesis that nivolumab plus ipilimumab would have clinical activity in patients with mCRPC. However, neither the signal-seeking portion nor the randomized portion of the trial were designed to statistically compare between cohorts, and sample sizes in the randomized portion were not based on statistical power calculations. Initially, the randomized portion of the trial was planned with two parts: part 1, to assess the optimal dose(s) for the nivolumab plus ipilimumab combination and to identify potential biomarker(s) of response, and part 2, to further investigate the identified optimal dose(s) and biomarker(s) in an expanded patient population. However, based on slow enrollment and changing priorities for the study sponsor, the randomized portion was altered via a protocol amendment to focus on assessing two alternative nivolumab plus ipilimumab regimens, ipilimumab monotherapy, and cabazitaxel, again with no planned statistical analyses. Per this protocol amendment, approximately 259 patients with postchemotherapy mCRPC were planned for randomization across the four new cohorts (74, 74, 37, and 74 patients in the N3I1, N1I3, I-mono, and CABA cohorts, respectively) with the number of patients with non-measurable disease at baseline capped at 105, so the remaining 154 patients (44, 44, 22, and 44 patients in the N3I1, N1I3, I-mono, and CABA cohorts, respectively) would have measurable disease at baseline. Although the overall sample sizes were not related to any statistical power calculations, the number of enrolled patients with measurable disease was based on an expected ORR of approximately 30% in the N3I1 and/or N1I3 cohorts (i.e., 13 responders among the 44 treated patients), which would give a two-sided 95% CI of 16.8% to 45.2%, with the lower CI (16.8%) being higher than the expected ORR for the CABA cohort (estimated at approximately 15% based on the TROPIC study8). This analysis represents the first protocol-specified analysis of the new cohorts, performed after approximately 90% of randomized patients had approximately 9 months of minimum follow-up.

ORRs, PSA responses, and corresponding 95% CIs were calculated using the Clopper and Pearson method; rPFS, time to and duration of objective and PSA responses, and OS were estimated using Kaplan–Meier methodology. Patient demographics/clinical characteristics, exposure, and safety data were reported using descriptive statistics. Data presented here for the N3I1 cohort are based only on the patients originally randomized to that cohort, and not to patients crossing over from the I-mono and CABA cohorts. For the I-mono and CABA cohorts, all presented data except OS are those collected before receipt of first N3I1 dose among any crossover patients; OS data for the I-mono and CABA cohorts are presented for the entire treatment period, regardless of crossover to the N3I1 cohort. Data analysis was completed using SAS 9.2 for Unix.

sec.title: CODEX and TCGA analyses
sec.p: Tumor samples were stained using a CODEX panel of commercial- or lab-conjugated antibodies (Supplementary Table 11). Four-micron FFPE tissue sections underwent antigen retrieval using ER2, pH9 on the Leica BondRX and slides were stained with a mixture of conjugated antibodies either overnight at 4 °C or for 3 h at room temperature. Whole section images were acquired on Phenocycler-Fusion (Akoya Bioscience), using DAPI, ATTO-550, AF647, and AF750 channels, and images were processed through version 2.2.0. to generate QPTIFF files for analysis. Processed CODEX images were uploaded to Enable Medicine portal where the DeepCell cell segmentation was performed using DAPI channel to identify nuclei, and the nuclear masks were dilated to obtain whole-cell segmented cells (number of dilations = 10, cell threshold = 400 µm). Next, QC filtration (based on cell size, signal sum, nuclear signal, and signal coefficient of variation) and normalization using Leiden clustering (min dist = 0.1, resolution = 0.3 or 0.25; neighbors = 50) were performed. For annotations, the normalized cluster biomarker expression was plotted and visualized by generating a heatmap. Cluster spatial information was overlaid on sample images. Annotations were assigned for each cluster based on the visual confirmation of biomarker expression on multiplexed images32. For the CODEX assay and analyses, all measurements were taken from distinct tissue samples, no samples were measured repeatedly, and all samples were depleted.

The perivascular immune niches were measured as a density by counting the frequency of niches per mm2 area in all samples. Density was compared using the Mann–Whitney unpaired test. To determine cell-cell interactions, an algorithm to determine cell distance for a given cell type pair and the average minimum distance was calculated32. The algorithm proceeds as follows: for each cell i of cell type A, compute distances to all cells of type B (rdist::cdist); for each i, compute the shortest distance to a cell of type B (the minimum distance); and compute the average of all cells i in each region of interest. Finally, to compare this metric between patient cohorts, we performed Welch two-sample t-tests (GraphPad Prism 10) on the average minimum distance metric between cellular interactions of different clusters32. The enablemedicine.com website was used to access the Enable Medicine portal to run the above analyses’ cell-cell interaction pipeline.

For the survival analysis associated with the CODEX data, niche signatures were identified by locating differentially expressed genes in the cell types within the interaction niche, comparing interactive cell types as one group against the other cell types (see the CODEX methods section). Specifically, we used prostate cancer single-cell data4 to identify differentially expressed genes enriched in the cell types of the perivascular immune niche versus all other cell types. An unpaired, two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test was used for the differential expression test. The top five genes were selected based on their fold change from the list of differentially expressed genes that met the following criteria: Bonferroni-corrected P < 0.0001, average expression fold change >2, and upregulated expression in the target group compared to the rest. These genes were used for subsequent cancer outcome analysis.

We used TCGA dataset as a validation cohort for survival analysis. We identified 484 patients from TCGA-PRAD by downloading RNA-seq count data and clinical follow-up information from the Genomic Data Commons data portal (Project: TCGA-PRAD, https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov). From the original 500 cases, we retained only primary adenocarcinoma, not otherwise specified specimens with complete survival data and matched submitter IDs, yielding 484 patients. OS was used for all survival analyses. Raw counts were normalized and then z-score transformed across the full cohort. For each patient, enrichment scores were calculated using the top five genes, incorporating two additional genes, CCL19 and CCL21, associated with perivascular niches33 using the GSVA package in R34. The z-transformed niche signature scores were dichotomized into high and low groups based on the median score. The niche signature scores were then analyzed using a Cox proportional hazards model, and a Kaplan–Meier curve was plotted for survival analysis with the R package survival.
